SGB is SCGSim's semantic geometry construction process: it combines layout shapes, materials, electrical assignments and contact relationships into one geometry that can be built.
The former surface-distance-band design is retained below as a historical reference.
Bands are geometric partitions, not an automatic operation on every surface; the original materials, terminals and adjacent volumes must remain consistent after partitioning.

This page follows one public example through **source → planning → CAD and meshing**.
For the formal API and capability boundaries, see the [semantic geometry contract](../geometry-sgb.qmd); for module responsibilities, see [architecture and data flow](../architecture.qmd).

::: {.callout-note title="This page focuses on the Gmsh/Palace geometry path"}
The main path described here builds CAD with Gmsh/OCC, generates a mesh with Gmsh and passes it to Palace.
AEDT also uses source semantics and physical representations, but builds its project through the native AEDT Modeler; the semantic goals are similar, while construction and execution follow each backend's own contract.
:::

## Source stage: state the model's facts first {#source-stage}

### What shapes, process data and assembly each contribute

A user typically selects a component from a component library and creates a layout with GDSFactory.
The component supplies its local shapes and their purpose: which region is a metal pad, which region supplies a junction, and which functional regions a port refers to. A GDS containing outlines alone cannot supply these meanings.
These local declarations are reused with the component, rather than inferred from object names after a solver has created them.

A **PDK (process design kit)** provides components and process information.
Its materials and layer stack define layer mappings, materials, conductor or solution-region roles, Z positions, thicknesses and the actual supporting bodies.
An explicit process mapping therefore connects “which layer is drawn” to “which material occupies that location in three dimensions.”

Here, an **assembly model** means the model a user creates by placing multiple components together and adding declarations that span them.
Two conductors on the same PDK metal layer can belong to Net A and Net B: the process supplies material and height, while the assembly model separately declares their final electrical assignments.

The assembly model places the components and declares the final Nets, substrate/vacuum regions, physical representation and requested surface partitions.
A Net is an electrical collection explicitly declared by the user; geometric contact does not rewrite that assignment.
A shared Net name also does not replace subsequent checks of actual geometric contact.

::: {.callout-important title="A short between different Nets stops preparation"}
Under the current contact rules, recognized coplanar face contact or conductor-volume overlap across different Nets stops preparation with a short-circuit error, preserving the original Net declarations.
Ordinary degenerate edge/point-only contacts are also rejected; a lateral seam within the same Net and effective film has a specific exception, described in the [semantic geometry contract](../geometry-sgb.qmd).

If a direct electrical connection is intended, explicitly assign both conductors to the same Net first, then let the contact rules validate the geometry; a shared Net neither skips validation nor guarantees that every contact is acceptable.
:::

::: {#source-grid .callout-important title="Source DBU, shared XY precision and film thickness are different settings"}
The GDS **database unit (DBU)** sets the coordinate increment the source can represent; when using GDSFactory, set the source DBU before creating components.
`GeometryPlan` uses the actual emitted DBU when `grid_size_um=None`; an explicitly different value fails rather than changing the component library's global settings.
The shared grid applies to assembled XY/layer polygons; Z, film thickness and the later finite-element mesh size each have a separate meaning.

Even when source endpoints lie on the grid, computed intersections may not: the segment from $(0,0)$ to $(3,1)$ nm intersects $x=1$ nm at $(1,\frac13)$ nm. Rotation can also produce off-grid coordinates.
:::

### One model followed throughout the page

The example has two separate metal pieces: the left one has a hole and an upper-right notch, while the right one has no hole. They are assigned to Net A and Net B, respectively.
A complete rectangular **lumped port** is requested between them, providing a defined surface for a lumped electrical condition between the two terminals.
The central port is not a metal bridge that merges A and B into one Net; any metal needed to complete a terminal belongs to that terminal's original owner.

This public example starts directly from normalized source geometry input, rather than creating a new GDSFactory component on this page.
The source, planning and CAD views below all continue from that same input; a component frontend first lowers its input to the same source boundary.
The example code is in the [rectangular-junction and hole fixture](https://github.com/OrPenStrike/scgsim/blob/2ed85adc/tests/test_rectangular_junction_geometry.py#L230).

Start with the original left metal in @fig-sgb-source. P1–P6 are its six authored exterior corners, and H1–H4 are the hole corners; coordinates are in µm.

::: {#fig-sgb-source .askr-wide-figure}
```{=html}
<iframe src="../images/sgb-concept/en-source-xy.html" title="Original source: six exterior corners and four hole corners of the left metal" width="100%" height="640" style="border:0;" loading="lazy"></iframe>
```

Original source: six exterior corners and four hole corners of the left metal
:::

The left metal's **outer ring** follows these points in order and closes back to its start; the **inner ring** encloses an area without metal.
The upper-right notch opens to the exterior, whereas the hole is entirely surrounded by metal. They play different roles in subsequent contact and distance calculations.

```text
Outer ring: P1(-2,0) → P2(3,0) → P3(3,1) → P4(2,1)
            → P5(2,2) → P6(-2,2) → back to P1
Inner ring: H1(-1.5,0.5) → H2(-0.5,0.5) → H3(-0.5,1.5)
            → H4(-1.5,1.5) → back to H1
Units: µm
```

The original left metal has a bounding rectangle of 10 µm²; subtracting the 1 µm² upper-right notch and the 1 µm² hole leaves 8 µm² of metal.
Changing the hole changes this shape; moving the whole component changes its assembly position; changing its Net changes an electrical declaration without moving or joining the shape automatically.

@fig-sgb-source-context shows the two metal pieces in plan view and the projection of the surrounding regions. Their vertical material relationship is shown later in @fig-sgb-physical.

::: {#fig-sgb-source-context .askr-wide-figure}
```{=html}
<iframe src="../images/sgb-concept/en-context-xy.html" title="The complete source layout" width="100%" height="640" style="border:0;" loading="lazy"></iframe>
```

The complete source layout
:::

At this point, we know the source objects and shapes. The finite-thickness conductor has not yet been represented as a sheet, the junction terminals have not been completed, and distance bands have not been added.

### Turn source facts into named objects {#entity-occurrence-and-net}

To keep referring to “this metal piece on the left” throughout preparation, SCGSim describes it as an **Entity** named `chip/left`.
An Entity associates source shape, purpose and material; the substrate and vacuum regions also have Entities, so an Entity does not inherently mean a conductor.
Here, `chip/left` and `chip/right` are bound to the final Nets A and B, separately from the polygon point lists.

The same component can be placed twice; each placement is a **component occurrence**.
The assembly model distinguishes them by occurrence paths, translation and rotation, so that pads with the same local name still refer to the correct placed metal.
The component definition retains local identities, while the assembly model explicitly assigns final Nets across components.

Source preparation combines this information with the material stack into a fixed copy called a **snapshot**.
Editing the original component later does not change an existing snapshot; prepare again to use the new shape.
This is the common source starting point for interface catalogues, distance bands and backend construction.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Corresponding public interfaces"}
The component frontend gathers its sources through `GeometryPlan(component=..., root_id=..., layer_stack=..., material_records=..., coupon_padding_um=...)`.
`register_instance(path, reference)` binds an actual component occurrence, `plan.entities` exposes named Entities, and `set_nets(...)` takes the final `Net → Entity ID` mapping.
`prepare()` returns a `GeometryPlanSnapshot`; the normalized input supplied directly by this example is a `GeometryBuildInput`. See the [component-to-backend contract](../geometry-sgb.qmd#component-to-backend-geometry-contract) for the full sequence.
:::

## Planning stage: determine the physical geometry to build {#planning-stage}

### A film has source thickness; a sheet has a real attachment plane

The source model describes process objects; the simulation model must also choose how to represent them.
It can retain a conductor's actual thickness, or use an explicit physical representation to map a film to a zero-thickness conductor sheet attached to its supporting surface.
That choice uses the source material layer and attachment relationship, rather than moving metal to whichever plane looks closest.

The source metal film in this example occupies $z\in[0,0.25]$ µm. With the `substrate_face` representation, the effective conductor sheet lies on the substrate's upper surface at $z=0$.
The source thickness describes the process film, while the zero-thickness sheet describes the representation being built; these values refer to different stages and do not conflict.
@fig-sgb-physical shows the materials and conductor at $y=0.25$ µm. It opens in “Film detail”; select “Full section” to inspect the substrate and surrounding vacuum.
Select “Effective: sheet” to compare the effective conductor sheet.
The close-up uses different display scales on its two axes; read positions and thicknesses from the coordinates.

::: {#fig-sgb-physical .askr-wide-figure}
```{=html}
<iframe src="../images/sgb-concept/en-cross-section.html" title="Source film and effective sheet: switch between material cross-sections" width="100%" height="640" style="border:0;" loading="lazy"></iframe>
```

Source film and effective sheet: switch between material cross-sections
:::

In both the source and effective views of @fig-sgb-physical, `substrate` is Si in $z\in[-2,0]$ µm, and `upper_air` is the upper vacuum region in $z\in[0,4.25]$ µm.
`lower_air` surrounds the sides of the substrate over the same lower height range; the entire lower half is not replaced with Si.
Planning must therefore retain both the planar shapes and the materials above, below and beside them.

### Why the junction needs a complete rectangle and terminal supports

A Josephson junction can use a lumped representation in an electromagnetic model, with a specified port surface carrying the lumped electrical condition between its two terminals.
This stage constructs the geometry; the backend still assigns inductance through the existing port name, rather than inferring it from shape.
The example requests a complete central rectangle connected to two selected metal terminals, giving the port's full width a defined terminal contact support.

The request identifies the source sheet, both terminal Entities/occurrences and their Nets.
Planning derives the central rectangle and terminal-owned end metals only for this explicit request and its actual attachment plane; it does not fill arbitrary gaps automatically.
The original left notch leaves the requested terminal support incomplete, so an additional region $[2,3]\times[1,2]$ µm is derived. It fills the upper-right notch in @fig-sgb-source and remains in Net A.
@fig-sgb-effective shows the original outline dashed and the left end addition in orange; the added metal still belongs to Net A.

::: {#fig-sgb-effective .askr-wide-figure}
```{=html}
<iframe src="../images/sgb-concept/en-effective-xy.html" title="Left terminal completion: original outline, added metal and retained hole" width="100%" height="640" style="border:0;" loading="lazy"></iframe>
```

Left terminal completion: original outline, added metal and retained hole
:::

The left support thus grows from 8 µm² to $8+1=9$ µm², retaining its hole.
Its new exterior is the rectangle $[-2,3]\times[0,2]$ µm; the original P5 remains on its upper boundary but is no longer a corner.
The seam between original and added metal disappears inside their union and is no longer a physical edge.

@fig-sgb-effective-port shows the full width of the same junction: the central rectangle covers $x\in[3,7]$, $y\in[0,2]$ µm.
The right end addition belongs to Net B, while the central port remains distinct from the metal at either end.
Interface recognition and distance bands use this final support geometry, rather than partitioning the old outline and adding terminal metal afterward.

::: {#fig-sgb-effective-port .askr-wide-figure}
```{=html}
<iframe src="../images/sgb-concept/en-port-xy.html" title="Complete central port and terminal metal ownership" width="100%" height="640" style="border:0;" loading="lazy"></iframe>
```

Complete central port and terminal metal ownership
:::

### One geometric surface can carry two material interfaces {#regions-and-boundaries}

A material interface describes what is on either side of a surface, not just a label on a plane.
The substrate lies below the left metal in this example and vacuum lies above it, so the same support plane carries both metal–substrate (MS) and metal–air (MA) meanings.
A substrate–air (SA) interface can also occur between substrate and vacuum.

Shared geometry does not imply a shared field side: MS retains the substrate side, MA retains the vacuum side, and each retains its own material coefficients and selection.
The band shapes can therefore be shared while the two interfaces' field-energy calculations remain separate; equal areas do not make their results identical or justify counting them twice.

An exterior boundary is another case: a wall of the outer vacuum enclosure may belong to just one solution volume.
It retains its actual construction surface and owner, without inventing a second material merely to obtain an interface name.
Partitioning must retain this kind of wall's original parent–child relationship as well.

### Shared topology gives adjacent surfaces the same edge

The intersection example in the [source-precision note](#source-grid) explains the planning problem: if adjacent surfaces round their intersections independently, one original edge can acquire two sets of nodes.

SGB uses one shared noded network in assembly XY, retaining the source object, ring and segment of every original directed edge.
Intersections and the native grid algorithm's near-vertex events first form subdivided source-edge paths; coincident edges retain all origins and directions.
Membership transitions across those edges then determine the ownership of each complete cell, without sampling its centre or guessing from the nearest edge.

:::: {.askr-wide-figure aria-label="Source edges form one shared noded network; parent surfaces and bands use the same atomic cells"}
::: {.askr-mermaid-view view-label="View the shared subdivision"}
```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  S["Named source boundaries<br/>Outer ring, inner rings, direction"] --> N["Shared noded network"]
  N --> E["Shared atomic edges<br/>Retain every source origin"]
  E --> C["Complete atomic cells<br/>Membership from directed edges"]
  C --> P["Reconstruct parent surfaces"]
  C --> B["Select distance bands"]
  R["Original physical shapes"] -. "Hole, component and contact checks" .-> P
```
:::
::::

The parents and bands in the diagram use the same cells, with no independent second rounding during reconstruction.
This **shared topology** gives adjacent geometry common points and edges; the original shapes remain available separately for hole, connected-component and contact checks.
If source paths, directions or memberships cannot be established uniquely, preparation fails explicitly rather than filling holes with a tolerance or deleting small regions.

### Historical design: SGB surface-distance bands (withdrawn) {#distance-bands}

This section records an earlier design only. The current SCGSim source does not expose its geometry producer, so the API examples below are not current usage instructions. Native Palace Mask/Inset margins remain separate and require a Palace executable that supports them.

The user first selects an actual **parent surface** from the effective model's surface catalogue, then specifies its source ownership, cut distances and original edges that define the distance origin.
A parent is not a plane guessed from a metal name: the same object can have several surfaces, hole rings and walls.
Selecting all original edges includes both exterior and hole rings; an explicit subset uses only those selected original edges.

Here, the selected parent is the left support after terminal completion in @fig-sgb-effective, retaining its adjacency to the substrate and upper vacuum.
On this plane, $d$ is the planar distance to the selected original boundary. Cuts at 0.125 and 0.25 µm produce the three disjoint bands in @fig-sgb-bands.
These two distances are explicit requests for this example, not automatic defaults for every model.

::: {#fig-sgb-bands .askr-wide-figure}
```{=html}
<iframe src="../images/sgb-concept/en-planned-bands.html" title="Planned distance bands on the completed left parent surface" width="100%" height="640" style="border:0;" loading="lazy"></iframe>
```

Planned distance bands on the completed left parent surface
:::

The parent in @fig-sgb-bands is the completed rectangle minus its hole, with a total area of 9 µm².
Bands also form around the hole. Concave corners or holes can give a band more than one connected component, so the three bands produce six child surfaces here.
P1, P2, P5 and P6 remain as reference points on the exterior boundary.

::: {.askr-table-compact .askr-table-numeric}
| Band | Range | Child surfaces | Area (µm²) |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| C0 | $0\le d<0.125$ | 2 | 2.236324 |
| C1 | $0.125\le d<0.25$ | 1 | 2.209366 |
| C2 | $d\ge0.25$ | 3 | 4.554310 |
:::

To inspect “at least 0.125 µm from the boundary,” select C1 and C2; “at least 0.25 µm” selects C2 alone.
These cumulative selections overlap, so their separately calculated results cannot be added as though the regions were disjoint.
The partition retains the original hole and the small connected regions within each band.

::: {.callout-note title="Partition seams are not new distance origins"}
Distance origins come from the parent's original physical boundary.
Neither the internal seam removed by the metal/end union nor the new seams between distance bands become additional edges from which to inset again.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Pass the selection request to the source plan"}
Use `surface_distance_band_catalogue(...)` to read actual parents from the corresponding construction plan, create a `SurfaceDistanceBandSpec`, then pass it to later snapshots through `GeometryPlan.set_surface_distance_bands(...)`.
The catalogue name of this example's parent is `SURF__MS__chip/left__substrate__upper_air__0000`; `boundary_segments=None` includes all original exterior and hole edges, while an explicit subset uses `SourceBoundarySegment`.
The example starts from normalized input and adds the same request with `with_surface_distance_bands(...)`. See the [planar distance-band contract](../geometry-sgb.qmd#surface-distance-bands) for exact parameters.
:::

### Connect caps, hole walls and exterior walls to the same nodes

Distance bands are more than a display mask: they create real partition surfaces that subsequent CAD and meshing must respect.
If a band adds a node to the upper cap, the sidewall and opposite cap must follow the same incident edge chain, or the volume boundary becomes inconsistent.
SGB therefore retains the mapping from original edges to realized shared chains and propagates nodes to every incident surface.

Wall distances are still classified in the original parent's plane and then mapped to realized facets through the existing construction correspondence; this does not introduce a different three-dimensional distance metric.
Z and film thickness are not rounded again by the XY grid.
This example's plan contains 12 such solution-region wall facets, which enclose three volumes together with their caps.

Complete surfaces are also organized into shared points, curves and ordered loops.
T-junctions and collinear overlapping edges are split into shared atomic curves; when two surfaces use the same edge in opposite directions, they retain directional references rather than creating another approximate edge.
Outer and inner loops bound each surface, and oriented surface references enclose a shell for each volume.

Before CAD construction, planning checks parent–child source relationships, materials and ownership, port adjacency, volume closure and group coverage.
An actual exterior wall can be a geometric parent, while a material interface retains its interface identity; a complete parent replaced by children is not built again as another live surface.
Adding bands thus changes the partition without silently adding material or losing original boundaries.

## Construction and meshing: turn the plan into a native model {#construction-stage}

### Build CAD from shared points and surfaces

Planning has already determined materials, terminals, adjacent volumes and shared surfaces. OCC (Open CASCADE) realizes those relationships as CAD.
The polygon path builds points, lines, curve loops and planes into shells and volumes, with incident volumes sharing one surface rather than separately constructing overlapping lookalikes.
That is why shared topology is established first, instead of asking a final global CAD fragment operation to guess material ownership.

This example passes the same effective input with its bands to the existing builder, which produces XAO geometry, physical groups and adjacency information.
@fig-sgb-native-3d shows the full model's native wireframe and curve endpoints read after reopening that XAO; @fig-sgb-native-bands separately colours the selected parent's distance bands.

::: {#fig-sgb-native-3d .askr-wide-figure}
```{=html}
<iframe src="../images/sgb-concept/en-native-cad-3d.html" title="Actual XAO: native curves and selected bands in the three-volume model" width="100%" height="720" style="border:0;" loading="lazy"></iframe>
```

Actual XAO: native curves and selected bands in the three-volume model
:::

The three volumes in @fig-sgb-native-3d are the Si substrate, upper vacuum and vacuum beside the substrate.
The plan contains 118 points, 132 curves and 26 live surfaces; these have entered actual CAD construction, rather than remaining only a planning drawing.

### Follow the same surface across native renumbering

@fig-sgb-native-bands shows the native band edges and endpoints of the same left parent as @fig-sgb-bands, with colours corresponding to the same C0/C1/C2 bands.
Rotate this three-dimensional view to see the shared $z=0$ plane. It displays read-back curves and endpoints, without adding invented filled CAD surfaces.
Each band child is associated with a group through a stable name and retains native adjacency to the substrate and upper vacuum.

::: {#fig-sgb-native-bands .askr-wide-figure}
```{=html}
<iframe src="../images/sgb-concept/en-native-bands-3d.html" title="Actual XAO: native band edges and nodes on the selected left parent" width="100%" height="720" style="border:0;" loading="lazy"></iframe>
```

Actual XAO: native band edges and nodes on the selected left parent
:::

CAD import renumbers integer **tags**, so “surface 19” is not a permanent name across export and import.
For example, the following children become surfaces 7 and 8 in this import, but their full group names still identify the same geometry and adjacent volumes.

::: {.askr-table-compact .askr-table-numeric}
| Stable child-name suffix | Exported surface tag | Imported surface tag | Adjacent volumes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `__DIST_0000_0000` | 19 | 7 | `substrate`, `upper_air` |
| `__DIST_0001_0000` | 27 | 8 | `substrate`, `upper_air` |
:::

Each full name begins with the selected left parent's name, while a native tag is meaningful only within its particular model.
Native surfaces outside the physical groups remain CAD diagnostic data; they do not automatically become additional solver surfaces.

### Meshing respects the geometry already established

The Palace mesh builder reads the XAO, groups and controls in a fresh Gmsh process.
`gmsh_default` uses Gmsh's native sizing behaviour without injecting SCGSim custom size fields. Holes, ports and bands are still real geometric constraints and affect the mesh.
A small cut distance therefore adds more than an integration option: it can also add CAD partitions and conformal-meshing work.

After three-dimensional mesh generation, checks still cover tetrahedra in solution volumes, conformity between port and volume faces, and node contact between ports and conductor boundaries.
Only after these checks does the solver receive `palace.msh` and its group mapping.
The worked example here reaches CAD/XAO and native adjacency; continue with the [Palace tutorial](../course/palace-eigenmode.qmd) for three-dimensional meshing and field solutions.

## What a shared source covers—and what remains separate {#a-shared-source-has-a-specific-reach}

A shared source lets Palace and AEDT use the same named objects, Nets, materials and physical-representation requests. Each backend still follows its own port and execution contracts to prepare a native project.
The same source does not make construction plans for different physical representations interchangeable, or promise a separate native integral for every source Entity.

### Polygons and explicit curves {#explicit-curved-boundaries}

An ordinary GDS contour that approximates an arc is still a polygon with vertices.
Explicitly declared arcs and other curves follow a separate OCC path that retains curve intent and native mappings; that path currently supports neither surface-distance bands nor Route C.
To choose a representation and backend, consult the contracts for [physical representation](../geometry-sgb.qmd#physical-representation), [explicit curves](../geometry-sgb.qmd#source-curves) and [surface-distance bands](../geometry-sgb.qmd#surface-distance-bands).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Public example and figure sources"}
This page uses the public rectangular-junction, hole and band example, together with curves, groups and adjacency read from the same XAO construction.
The [case data index](../images/sgb-concept/public-case-binding.json) records the source version and stage mappings; follow the source, planning and CAD stages on this page when reading the figures.
:::
